title: How do Broadcast Joins interact with AQE — AQE can dynamically switch from SSMJ to BHJ at runtime when it discovers a post-filter table is small enough, even if the initial plan chose SSMJ?
shortTitle: How Broadcast Joins interact with AQE — runtime switch from SSMJ to BHJ

s1_definition.profdef: Adaptive Query Execution can convert a planned Shuffle Sort Merge Join into a Broadcast Hash Join at runtime when the actual materialized size of a join side, measured after an earlier stage completes, turns out to be below the broadcast threshold. The static planner may choose a sort-merge join because its compile-time estimate was too large or unavailable, but once a filter or aggregation runs and AQE sees the real, smaller size in the shuffle statistics, it rewrites the remaining plan to broadcast that side, avoiding the sort and merge.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India plans a big matching job assuming a report is huge, so it schedules the slow sort-and-merge approach. But partway through, after filtering the report to only this month's entries, the clerk sees it is actually just two pages. Adaptive Query Execution is the supervisor who notices this mid-job and says "stop — that is tiny now, just photocopy it for everyone and match locally," switching from the slow plan to the fast broadcast on the spot, using what was actually observed rather than the original guess.
s1_definition.oneliner: AQE watches real runtime sizes and upgrades a planned sort-merge join to a broadcast join when a side turns out small enough after filtering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Adaptive Query Execution can convert a planned Shuffle Sort Merge Join into a Broadcast Hash Join at runtime when the actual materialized size of a join side, measured after an earlier stage completes, turns out to be below the broadcast threshold. The static planner may choose a sort-merge join because its compile-time estimate was too large or unavailable, but once a filter or aggregation runs and AQE sees the real, smaller size in the shuffle statistics, it rewrites the remaining plan to broadcast that side, avoiding the sort and merge.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India plans a big matching job assuming a report is huge, so it schedules the slow sort-and-merge approach. But partway through, after filtering the report to only this month's entries, the clerk sees it is actually just two pages. Adaptive Query Execution is the supervisor who notices this mid-job and says "stop — that is tiny now, just photocopy it for everyone and match locally," switching from the slow plan to the fast broadcast on the spot, using what was actually observed rather than the original guess.

**One line to remember:** AQE watches real runtime sizes and upgrades a planned sort-merge join to a broadcast join when a side turns out small enough after filtering.

sections.s2_technical:
The static Catalyst planner decides join strategies before the job runs, using compile-time size estimates. Those estimates are often wrong for a side whose size depends on a filter or an aggregation the planner cannot evaluate ahead of time. So the planner conservatively picks a Shuffle Sort Merge Join, which is always safe for large sides. Without AQE, that choice is final, even if the side turns out tiny at runtime.

Adaptive Query Execution changes this by re-optimizing at stage boundaries. When an earlier stage finishes — for example the stage that filters a dimension — AQE reads the actual sizes of the shuffle outputs from the map statistics. If one join side's real materialized size is now at or below the adaptive broadcast threshold, AQE rewrites the remaining physical plan to use a Broadcast Hash Join instead of the sort-merge it originally planned. It broadcasts the now-known-small side and skips the shuffle, sort, and merge on the large side. This is sometimes called a dynamic join strategy switch, and it is one of AQE's headline optimizations.

The key difference from static auto-broadcast is the timing and the information. Static auto-broadcast decides from estimates before running; AQE decides from measured sizes after a stage runs. That measured size is accurate, so AQE can confidently broadcast a side that the static planner could not, because the static planner only knew the pre-filter size. This is why a query can show a sort-merge join in the pre-run explain output but a broadcast hash join in the Spark UI's final executed plan.

A senior-level nuance is the configuration and limits. The switch is governed by the adaptive settings, including the adaptive broadcast threshold which may differ from the static autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, and AQE must be enabled. The switch only happens at a stage boundary where AQE has real statistics, so a side whose size is only known mid-stage will not trigger it. There is also a local shuffle reader optimization that pairs with the switch: when AQE broadcasts the small side, it can read the already-shuffled large side locally without a network fetch, further cutting cost. And because AQE can change the plan, the authoritative view of what ran is the Spark UI final plan, not the static explain. The practical benefit is that you often do not need to hand-tune broadcast hints for post-filter cases, because AQE catches them automatically.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India joins the huge transactions table to a product dimension. The product dimension is fifty megabytes on disk, above the threshold, so the static planner chooses a sort-merge join. This is the conservative static decision.

Problem 2 — At runtime, the query filters products to active ones, leaving only three megabytes. After that filter stage completes, AQE reads the real three-megabyte size, which is below the adaptive broadcast threshold, and switches the join to a broadcast hash join, skipping the sort-merge. This is exactly the AQE dynamic switch.

The demo models the planner choosing sort-merge from the pre-filter estimate, then an AQE re-optimization step that reads the post-filter size and flips the join to broadcast, logging the before-and-after plan and the saved shuffle.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a product dimension estimated at fifty megabytes but only three megabytes after filtering to active products, against a ten-megabyte adaptive broadcast threshold.

Step 1: Before running, the static planner uses the fifty-megabyte estimate. Fifty is above ten, so it plans a Shuffle Sort Merge Join — the conservative, safe choice given the estimate.

Step 2: The query runs the filter stage that reduces products to active ones. When that stage completes, its shuffle output size is measured and recorded in the map statistics.

Step 3: At the stage boundary, AQE reads the real size — three megabytes — which is now below the threshold. AQE rewrites the remaining plan to switch the join from sort-merge to a Broadcast Hash Join, broadcasting the three-megabyte side and adding a local shuffle reader so the large transactions side is read locally without a network fetch.

Step 4: The sort and merge on the huge transactions table are avoided entirely. The demo also shows a counter-case where accounts stays at six gigabytes after filtering, so AQE keeps the sort-merge join because the side is still large.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:51:00 [INFO] STATIC plan (before run): SortMergeJoin (estimate 50 MB > threshold)
2026-10-30 04:51:00 [INFO] ...filter stage runs, AQE reads real shuffle size at the stage boundary...
2026-10-30 04:51:00 [INFO] AQE plan (runtime): SWITCH to BroadcastHashJoin (runtime 3 MB <= threshold) + local shuffle reader on large side
2026-10-30 04:51:00 [INFO] Result: sort+merge on the huge transactions table avoided; small side broadcast instead.
2026-10-30 04:51:00 [INFO] STATIC plan: SortMergeJoin (estimate 8000 MB > threshold)
2026-10-30 04:51:00 [WARNING] AQE plan: keep SortMergeJoin (runtime 6000 MB still large)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Adaptive Query Execution interacts with broadcast joins by converting a planned sort-merge join into a broadcast hash join at runtime once it sees that a side is actually small. The static Catalyst planner chooses join strategies before the job runs, using compile-time estimates, and for a side whose size depends on a filter or aggregation the planner cannot evaluate ahead of time, it conservatively picks a sort-merge join because that is always safe. Without AQE that choice is final even if the side turns out tiny.

AQE re-optimizes at stage boundaries. When an earlier stage finishes, such as the stage that filters a dimension, AQE reads the real materialized sizes from the shuffle map statistics. If a join side's measured size is now at or below the adaptive broadcast threshold, AQE rewrites the remaining plan to broadcast that side and use a broadcast hash join instead of the sort-merge it originally planned, skipping the shuffle, sort, and merge on the large side. It also pairs this with a local shuffle reader so the already-shuffled large side is read locally without a network fetch. The crucial difference from static auto-broadcast is that AQE decides from measured sizes after a stage runs, which are accurate, rather than from pre-run estimates that only knew the pre-filter size.

At the National Bank of India this saved us from hand-tuning many broadcast hints. A join to a product dimension that was fifty megabytes on disk but only a few megabytes after filtering to active products was planned as a sort-merge, but with AQE enabled the pre-run explain showed a sort-merge while the Spark UI final plan showed a broadcast hash join, because AQE measured the small post-filter size and switched it. The practical points I stress are that AQE must be enabled, the switch only happens at a stage boundary where real statistics exist, the adaptive broadcast threshold governs it, and because AQE changes the plan, the authoritative view of what actually ran is the Spark UI final plan rather than the static explain output.
